feed.title: Combined summary - Decentralized Coinbase Payout Protocols (DCPP): A Framework for Discussion

entry.title: Combined summary - Decentralized Coinbase Payout Protocols (DCPP): A Framework for Discussion
entry.summary: Decentralized mining pools are undergoing a significant period of innovation, driven by renewed interest in protocols that enhance transparency, fairness, and security. Recent advancements focus on overcoming historical limitations, particularly the challenge of distributing coinbase payouts directly to a large number of miners. Protocols such as Stratum v2 (Sv2), DATUM, and the [Open Mining Stack](https://www.256foundation.org/) extend the groundwork established by early systems like P2Pool, yet must still contend with inherent scalability and technical constraints. The central bottleneck arises from block space and output slot limits, which prevent scaling native coinbase payouts to all contributors. This limitation not only affects how many miners can be paid per block but also exposes decentralized pools to new attack vectors, including payout settlement griefing (PSG) and identity-based manipulation known as the Rich List Attack (RLA). Three core design constraints shape the evolution of decentralized coinbase payout protocols (DCPPs). First, the limited number of available coinbase outputs makes direct payments to every miner unfeasible, especially as pool participation grows. Second, these payout mechanisms enlarge the attack surface, increasing the risk of unreliable or manipulated settlements. Third, Bitcoin’s scripting capabilities restrict the complexity of enforceable payout logic at the protocol level. As a result, when demand for payouts exceeds the number of available slots, pools typically prioritize top contributors—a method that invites abuse through identity splitting, where miners fragment their hashrate across multiple identities to gain additional slots. This undermines both fairness and the integrity of reward distribution. Multiple solutions have been proposed to address these vulnerabilities. Chris Belcher’s 2017 [payment hub model](https://bitcointalk.org/index.php?topic=2135429.0) introduced off-chain payment channels coordinated through a multisig-protected hub, mitigating some risks but remaining susceptible to identity laundering. Braidpool’s [Rolling Coinbase Aggregation (RCA)](https://github.com/braidpool/braidpool/blob/8d3c5198593d691f50ae5238cdaee215f4213cda/docs/braidpool_spec.mdpayout-update) batches rewards into single UTXOs, using threshold signatures from recent block-finding miners to authorize periodic payouts. Meanwhile, P2Poolv2 proposes a [market-driven mechanism](https://github.com/p2poolv2/p2poolv2/wiki/Payout-mechanism---Trading-Shares-For-Bitcoin) allowing atomic swaps of sharechain UTXOs for Lightning payments, aiming to aggregate enough value to justify direct coinbase allocations. All these models attempt to balance technical feasibility, security, and economic incentive, though each introduces its own set of trade-offs and persistent susceptibility to PSG and RLA. Ideal DCPP architectures envision proportional, independently enforceable claims for each participant, thus eliminating competition for ranked slots and discouraging identity splitting. In practice, current limitations in Bitcoin’s scripting and covenant abilities make such systems difficult to realize. Practical designs often rely on a blend of script-based controls and external market mechanisms, including coinpools funded from the coinbase and protected by pre-signed exit transactions. The governance of pooled outputs, selection of keyholders, and fallback procedures in case of absent or malicious actors remain open areas for research and development. Integrating structures like Spark and Ark within frameworks such as P2Poolv2 offers promising case studies, albeit with vulnerabilities such as the “poison pill” attack, where malicious participants inflate subtrees with identities to manipulate market makers. The adoption of standardized terminology—particularly PSG and RLA—has enhanced the clarity and precision of discourse surrounding decentralized mining pools. Historical analysis of P2Pool operations reveals that scaling challenges emerge naturally as network participation increases, independent of overt attacks. Data from as early as 2012 document hundreds of addresses being paid per block, with software-imposed limits (such as the 4,000-address cap) never reached in practice. Share difficulty and dust rules further constrained small miners, who disappeared from payout records when unable to meet minimum thresholds, a phenomenon arising from organic growth rather than malevolent action. Detailed payout data, including a CSV record of historic coinbase distributions, is available for review at [https://www.learnbitcoin.com/downloads/p2pool-coinbases.csv](https://www.learnbitcoin.com/downloads/p2pool-coinbases.csv). One solution proposed over a decade ago involves allowing miners to earn trustless shares, holding off on BTC payouts until a threshold is reached to avoid dust outputs. Despite advances, many contemporary protocols continue to reflect this foundational approach, demonstrating the enduring complexity of fair, scalable decentralized payout schemes. Strategic behavior by incumbents—such as splitting hash power among multiple accounts to appear as numerous small miners—remains an ongoing threat, as it enables subtle, deniable forms of griefing that degrade decentralized pool attractiveness without incurring significant costs.
